exhibits.title: Smelting Metal
exhibits.change: Fire pulled metal out of rock.
exhibits.context: Copper slag at Belovode in Serbia dates to about 5000 BCE, one of the earliest securely dated smelting sites. Smelting reduces copper ores with charcoal at around 1,100 °C. Metallurgy may have emerged in more than one place in the Balkans and Iran.
exhibits.significance: Metal could now be made in quantity and cast into any shape — the start of the ages named after metals.

uncertainty.note: Whether smelting was invented once and spread, or several times, is debated.

sources.note: Radivojević et al. 2010, J. Archaeological Science.

exhibits.title: The Sail

when.display: a mast-stepped boat model c. 5000 BCE; sails depicted in Egypt by c. 3200 BCE

exhibits.change: Wind, not muscle, began to move boats.
exhibits.context: A clay boat model with a socket for a mast from an Ubaid site in Kuwait suggests sailing in the Gulf around 5000 BCE. Egyptian images show sailing boats on the Nile by the late 4th millennium BCE.
exhibits.significance: The first use of a non-living energy source for transport — the basis of long-distance trade by water for the next 6,000 years.

uncertainty.note: Interpreting early models and images as sailing vessels is debated.

exhibits.title: Nabta Playa
exhibits.change: A ring of standing stones in the Sahara, raised by cattle herders.
exhibits.context: Pastoralists who used seasonal lakes in the then-greener eastern Sahara built stone arrangements and cattle burials. Some researchers propose astronomical alignments.
exhibits.significance: African pastoral societies shaped monuments long before the pyramids.

uncertainty.note: The dating and astronomical interpretation are disputed.

sources.note: Wendorf & Malville; Malville et al. 1998, Nature.

exhibits.title: The Potter's Wheel
exhibits.change: A spinning platform turned pot-making into a fast, repeatable craft.
exhibits.context: Slow turntables appear in the Near East in the 5th millennium BCE; true fast wheels using momentum developed later. Rotating motion on an axis came before the wheeled vehicle.
exhibits.significance: Mass production of standard vessels — and an early machine for rotation.

exhibits.title: The Plough
exhibits.change: Oxen dragging a scratch plough did the work of many hands.
exhibits.context: The ard, pulled by cattle, appears in images and in the traces of furrows by the 4th millennium BCE, as part of a wider shift to using animals for traction, milk and wool.
exhibits.significance: More land could be farmed by fewer people, with profound effects on labour and social structure.

exhibits.title: The First Cities

when.display: c. 4000–3100 BCE (Uruk); independently in several regions later

exhibits.change: Tens of thousands of strangers living together, fed by others' labour.
exhibits.context: By about 3100 BCE Uruk had tens of thousands of inhabitants, monumental temples, full-time specialists and administrators. Urban life arose independently in Egypt, the Indus, China, the Andes and Mesoamerica, each in its own form.
exhibits.significance: Cities concentrated people, ideas and power: most later inventions happened in or because of them.

uncertainty.note: What counts as the 'first city' depends on definitions; Uruk is the most widely cited early example.

exhibits.title: The Horse

when.display: horses managed c. 3500 BCE; modern domestic lineage spreads c. 2200 BCE

regions.note: Lower Volga–Don region, source of modern domestic horses (2021 genomic study).

exhibits.change: People harnessed an animal faster than any human.
exhibits.context: Horses at Botai were milked and possibly ridden around 3500 BCE, but genomics shows they are not the ancestors of today's domestic horses; that lineage spread from the western steppe around 2200 BCE, together with spoked-wheel chariots.
exhibits.significance: Horses transformed travel, communication, farming and warfare across Eurasia for four thousand years.

sources.note: Outram et al. 2009; Librado et al. 2021, Nature.

exhibits.title: The Wheel
exhibits.change: A disc turning on an axle: heavy loads rolled instead of dragged.
exhibits.context: Evidence for wheeled vehicles appears almost simultaneously across a wide area — Mesopotamia, the steppe and central Europe — within a few centuries after 3500 BCE, making the place of invention hard to pin down. Mesoamerican cultures made wheeled figurines but, without draught animals, did not use wheeled transport.
exhibits.significance: Wagons, chariots, mills, gears and turbines — rotation on an axle underlies much of later machinery.

uncertainty.note: Where the wheel was first invented is unknown; it spread remarkably fast.

exhibits.title: Writing

when.display: c. 3350–3200 BCE (Mesopotamia); invented independently at least three more times

regions.note: Egypt, c. 3250 BCE — independence from Mesopotamia debated.

exhibits.change: Speech became visible and permanent — memory outside the body.
exhibits.context: Proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk record grain, beer, livestock and labour. Within centuries signs came to stand for sounds, allowing writing of names, laws, letters and literature. Writing was invented separately in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica, and probably in Egypt; the Indus script remains undeciphered.
exhibits.significance: Writing let knowledge accumulate across generations and distances without a living teacher — the foundation of administration, law, history, science and literature.

uncertainty.note: How many independent inventions there were (Egypt especially) is debated.

exhibits.title: Bronze

regions.note: Bronze casting flourished from c. 1900 BCE; whether its origins were local or steppe-derived is debated.

exhibits.change: Copper alloyed with tin: harder, castable, and worth trading across continents.
exhibits.context: Arsenical copper came first; tin bronze spread from the late 4th millennium BCE. Tin deposits are rare and far from most copper, so bronze created long-distance trade networks reaching from Afghanistan and Cornwall to the Mediterranean.
exhibits.significance: Better tools and weapons — and trade networks that knitted distant societies together.

exhibits.title: Liangzhu's Dams
exhibits.change: A walled city with a system of dams and levees on a regional scale.
exhibits.context: Liangzhu, a Neolithic culture of the Yangtze delta, built a walled city of about 300 hectares and a hydraulic system of dams (around 3100 BCE) that managed floods and water transport. It also produced fine jade.
exhibits.significance: One of the earliest large-scale water engineering systems anywhere.

sources.note: Liu et al. 2017, PNAS. UNESCO World Heritage Site (2019).

exhibits.title: Egyptian Hieroglyphs
exhibits.change: Small labels from a royal tomb carry some of the earliest Egyptian signs.
exhibits.context: Bone and ivory labels from tomb U-j at Abydos bear signs used for sounds and places. Hieroglyphic writing developed into a system combining sound-signs and meaning-signs used for over 3,000 years.
exhibits.significance: Possibly a second, independent invention of writing, emerging at almost the same moment as cuneiform.

uncertainty.note: Whether Egyptian writing was invented independently or stimulated by contact with Mesopotamia is debated.

exhibits.title: Counting in Sixties

when.display: from c. 3200 BCE; fully positional by c. 2000 BCE

exhibits.change: A base-60 number system — the reason an hour has sixty minutes.
exhibits.context: Early Mesopotamian administrators used several counting systems for different goods; by the Old Babylonian period scribes used a place-value system in base 60 that allowed efficient calculation with fractions.
exhibits.significance: Place value, and our division of circles and hours, descend from this system.

exhibits.title: Stonehenge
exhibits.change: Giant stones hauled and raised to frame the solstice sun.
exhibits.context: Built in stages over some 1,500 years, Stonehenge aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Its bluestones were brought about 225 km from Wales.
exhibits.significance: Communal engineering and a calendar written in the landscape.

sources.note: English Heritage; Parker Pearson et al.

exhibits.title: The 365-Day Year

when.display: in use by the early 3rd millennium BCE (start uncertain)

exhibits.change: Twelve months of thirty days plus five extra — a civil year of 365 days.
exhibits.context: The Egyptian civil calendar was linked to the Nile flood and the heliacal rising of Sirius. It drifted against the seasons because it lacked a leap day, but its regularity made it useful for astronomers for millennia.
exhibits.significance: Ancestor of the Julian and Gregorian calendars used worldwide today.

uncertainty.note: The date of introduction is not documented.

exhibits.title: Papyrus

when.display: c. 2900 BCE (oldest blank roll); inscribed papyri by c. 2560 BCE

exhibits.change: A light, rollable writing surface made from a river reed.
exhibits.context: Sheets made from strips of papyrus pith were joined into rolls. The Wadi al-Jarf papyri, a logbook from the reign of Khufu, are the oldest inscribed papyri known.
exhibits.significance: Portable documents for administration and literature across the Mediterranean for three thousand years.

exhibits.title: Silk

when.display: silk textiles by c. 2700 BCE; traces reported much earlier

exhibits.change: Thread unwound from the cocoons of domesticated silkworms.
exhibits.context: Woven silk fragments from Qianshanyang date to around 2700 BCE; chemical traces of silk in older burials suggest an earlier start. Sericulture remained a Chinese secret for millennia.
exhibits.significance: Silk became one of the great luxury goods of Eurasian trade — giving the Silk Roads their name.

uncertainty.note: Claims of silk several thousand years older rely on indirect biochemical evidence.

exhibits.title: The Pyramids

when.display: c. 2650 BCE (Djoser); Great Pyramid c. 2560 BCE

exhibits.change: A state organised tens of thousands of workers to build mountains of cut stone.
exhibits.context: Djoser's step pyramid at Saqqara, attributed to the architect Imhotep, was followed within a century by the Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza, the tallest human-made structure for nearly 4,000 years. Workers' settlements show organised, fed and housed labour, not slaves in the popular sense.
exhibits.significance: A display of what surveying, logistics, record-keeping and centralised power could achieve.

exhibits.title: Caral
exhibits.change: Monumental platform mounds and plazas in the Americas, contemporary with the pyramids.
exhibits.context: Caral and neighbouring sites of the Supe Valley built pyramids, sunken circular plazas and residential sectors without pottery, supported by irrigated cotton and trade with fishing communities on the coast.
exhibits.significance: Urban, monumental society arose independently in South America as early as in the Old World.

exhibits.title: Cities of the Indus
exhibits.change: Planned grids, covered drains and uniform bricks and weights across a vast region.
exhibits.context: The Indus civilisation covered a larger area than Egypt or Mesopotamia. Its cities had standardised baked bricks, household bathrooms connected to street drains, and a precise, shared system of cubic stone weights. Its script remains undeciphered.
exhibits.significance: Urban planning and public sanitation on a scale not matched for millennia.

exhibits.title: Sea Trade of the Gulf
exhibits.change: Ships linked the Indus, Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia in regular trade.
exhibits.context: Mesopotamian texts name Meluhha, Magan and Dilmun as sources of copper, carnelian, timber and ivory. Indus seals and weights found in Mesopotamia and the Gulf confirm the connection.
exhibits.significance: One of the first regular long-distance maritime trade systems.

exhibits.title: Kerma
exhibits.change: A powerful Nubian kingdom with a giant mud-brick temple — the Western Deffufa.
exhibits.context: Kerma was the capital of the first Kingdom of Kush, a rival and trading partner of Egypt, with monumental architecture and elaborate royal burials.
exhibits.significance: Early African statehood beyond Egypt along the Nile.

exhibits.title: Glass

when.display: beads c. 2500 BCE; vessels c. 1500 BCE

exhibits.change: Sand and ash melted into a new, glossy, transparent material.
exhibits.context: Glass beads appear in Mesopotamia around 2500 BCE; core-formed glass vessels were made in Mesopotamia and Egypt from about 1500 BCE. Glassblowing came much later, around the 1st century BCE.
exhibits.significance: Without glass there are no lenses, spectacles, telescopes, microscopes, lab flasks or optical fibres.

exhibits.title: Written Law
exhibits.change: Rules and penalties written down, the same for every case.
exhibits.context: The Code of Ur-Nammu, from the Third Dynasty of Ur, is the oldest surviving law code. It set fines in silver for injuries — earlier than the more famous Code of Hammurabi.
exhibits.significance: Written law made justice more predictable and public.
